title: No Doesn't Mean No
html:
No doesn’t mean no. At least, not in the way we tend to think.

To be clear, I’m not saying that we should ignore no’s when doing so is blatantly unethical. But I am saying that we can often get what we want despite rejection.

For example, many of us know that when we asked our moms for ice cream and she said “No!”, she really meant “Ask your father”. Understanding this led me face-first into many a tub of peppermint bon bon. 

We can reframe no to mean “not yet,” “not like that,” or even “yes, but only if you ask your father.” Such reframing encourages us to restructure our approach and try again.

Using failures to update strategies was essential for my success in university. After scoring less than 50% on my first general chemistry exam, I wondered if a STEM major would be too challenging. Maybe I should have cut my losses there and pursued a degree in Gender and Women’s Studies.

Could I ever grok chemistry? Certainly, but not unless I changed my approach.

My current methods weren’t working, so I updated them until they produced the desired outcome. I received A’s on my remaining chemistry exams and finished top of the class in organic chemistry (a notorious weed-out class) the following year. 

In May 2024, I graduated with distinction with a double major in neurobiology and computer science. Gender and Women’s Studies my ass.

Simply put, we don’t need to take no for an answer.

After describing my comedic failures in the dating world to a Serbian friend of mine, she told me of a Serbian proverb: “Ne jebe uvek lep nego uporan".

“The handsome one doesn’t always fuck, but the persistent one does. / Ne jebe uvek lep nego uporan.” – Serbian Proverb
